Numbers in the left-hand column are the employer's to set — the finding arises when the file does not match the number the document promised.

facets.q: Does SNT-TC-1A require a written practice or only recommend one?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, but the written practice clause is one of its "shall" statements: the employer shall establish a written practice for the control and administration of NDT personnel training, examination and certification, the employer's NDT Level III shall review and approve it, and it shall be maintained on file. Codes and client specifications that invoke SNT-TC-1A make it contractually binding.

facets.q: Can we use a written practice template from another company?
facets.a: A template carries the other company's method list, hour figures, question counts and named Level III. Every one of those is a promise an auditor will check against your files. Templates are useful as structure and dangerous as content. Build the document against your own service menu, certificates and records — that is the whole substance of written practice development work.

facets.q: What passing grade should the written practice state?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A calls for a composite grade of at least 80 percent with no individual examination graded below 70 percent. For Level I and II the composite is the simple average of the general, specific and practical results. For Level III it is the simple average of the basic, method and specific results. A single flat pass mark describes a scheme the standard does not contain.

facets.q: How often do vision examinations have to be repeated?
facets.a: Under SNT-TC-1A (2020), near-vision acuity is examined annually: the candidate reads a minimum of Jaeger Number 2 or equivalent at the distance designated on the chart and not less than 12 in. (30.5 cm), with an Ortho-Rater minimum of 8 accepted as an alternative. Color contrast differentiation is demonstrated at initial certification and at five-year intervals afterwards.

facets.q: Who is allowed to administer a certification examination?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A states that examinations shall not be self-administered and shall not be administered by a person the candidate supervises. All in-house examination questions require the Level III's approval before use. A Level III who writes the questions, sits the specific examination and signs the result has generated three findings from one event. Independence is the reason many firms route Level III examination outside.

facets.q: What happens to a technician's certification when they leave the company?
facets.a: Employer-based certification is valid only within the employment relationship. Absent third-party certification, the certificate becomes void when employment ends, and the technician arrives at the next employer uncertified in that employer's terms. This is why the written practice needs a reinstatement clause stating what evidence transfers, what is re-examined, and who signs the new certification record.

sections.heading: A written practice is a commitment document, not a summary of the standard
paragraphs: Most rejected written practices fail for one reason: they restate SNT-TC-1A instead of committing to it. The recommended practice is drafted in "should" language and leaves the numbers open on purpose. ASNT's own guidance on employer-based certification puts it plainly — the employer replaces the advisory language with mandatory language, and the resulting document becomes a requirement inside the quality system. A written practice that copies "should" back out of the source has committed to nothing, and an auditor who reaches page three without finding a binding sentence already has a finding.

The document carries three fixed obligations. The employer shall establish it. The employer's NDT Level III shall review and approve it. It shall be maintained on file. Within that frame the employer may modify the basic provisions — training, experience, examination, recertification — but shall not eliminate them. Deleting the practical examination because specimens are inconvenient is not a modification, and dropping the recertification clause because nobody tracks dates is not a simplification. Both are eliminations, and both are written up.

This is also where firms decide whether to build or inherit. Companies producing the document from scratch work through written practice development against their own certificates, method list and record forms. Companies that download a template inherit somebody else's method list, somebody else's hour figures and somebody else's named Level III, then spend the audit explaining why none of it matches.

sections.heading: Scope: name the methods you sell, and nothing else
paragraphs: The scope section states which NDT methods the document governs, which codes and specifications the company works to, and which personnel it covers. Auditors test the boundary in both directions, and both directions hurt. A scope claiming eight methods when the company examines in three invites the auditor to ask for eight sets of training records, eight sets of examinations and eight qualified signatories. A scope naming three methods when a purchase order shows phased array work performed last quarter is a direct nonconformance: testing performed outside the certification program.

Write scope against the current service list and revise it when the service list changes. Adding TOFD means amending the written practice, obtaining the Level III's approval of the amendment, and completing training and examination records before the first job — in that order, not after. The sequence matters because the auditor reads dates. An amendment dated after the first TOFD report converts a paperwork lag into a finding about uncertified work.

Firms selling across maritime, offshore and fabrication normally run one document with a method matrix rather than separate practices per sector. The matrix is where maritime NDT consulting engagements start, because class society and owner specifications add requirements the base practice never contemplated — witness points, specimen types, approval routes — and those additions have to land somewhere the auditor can find them.

sections.heading: Level definitions: write duties, not dictionary entries
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A defines Level I as performing specific calibrations and examinations under specific written instructions, Level II as setting up and calibrating equipment, interpreting and evaluating results against codes and standards, preparing written instructions and training Level I personnel, and Level III as establishing techniques, interpreting codes and specifications, designating the method and technique to be used, and examining and certifying Level I and II personnel. Copying those three sentences is the floor. The written practices that pass audit go past it.

State what each level is authorized to sign inside your company. Name whether a Level II releases a final report without Level III review. Name whether a Level I performs a calibration unattended. Name which documents carry which signature. An auditor comparing a Level I's signature on a released report against a written practice that grants release authority to Level II holds a finding, and the finding lands on the company, not the technician.

This section is also where limited certifications get their boundaries. If the company certifies technicians for a restricted application — one technique, one geometry, one product line — say so, name the restriction, and make the certificate carry it. Unrestricted certificates issued against restricted training are the quiet version of the same problem, and they surface the first time a technician is asked to cover something the training never touched.

sections.heading: Education, training and experience: the numbers become binding
paragraphs: Table 6.3.1A of SNT-TC-1A lists initial training and experience hours for the employer to consider when writing the practice. Ultrasonic testing sits at 40 hours of organized training and 210 hours of experience in the method at Level I, with a further 40 training hours and 630 cumulative experience hours at Level II. Because the table is offered for consideration, the written practice can set different figures. What it cannot do is state a figure and then certify somebody short of it — that is the gap auditors open training records to find. Method-by-method hour figures are broken out in the NDT training hours guide.

Include the direct-to-Level-II route explicitly if you use it. SNT-TC-1A allows qualification directly to Level II with no time as a certified Level I, provided training and experience total the sum of the hours recommended for both levels. Written practices that stay silent on the route and then produce a Level II certificate with no Level I history hand the auditor a documentation gap. One sentence closes it.

Experience hours are hours in the method under qualified supervision, not hours on payroll. A record showing "employed since 2023" evidences nothing. The written practice should state the form experience is captured on — job type, method, hours, supervising signature — and who reviews it. That form is the artifact the auditor asks for by name, and the companies that designed it the week after an audit are the companies that failed one. Structured classroom hours delivered through corporate NDT training produce the training-hour side of the same record.

sections.heading: Examinations: structure, administration and grading
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A structures Level I and II qualification as a vision examination, a written general examination on the basic principles of the method, a written specific examination on the equipment, procedures and acceptance criteria used on the job, and a practical examination on representative specimens using at least one flawed specimen with a defined set of evaluation checkpoints. Level III qualification is structured as a basic examination, a method examination and a specific examination. The written practice names the question count for each written part and the checkpoint count for each practical.

Grading is the clause written wrong most often. SNT-TC-1A calls for a composite grade of at least 80 percent with no individual examination graded below 70 percent. For Level I and II the composite is the simple average of the general, specific and practical results. For Level III it is the simple average of the basic, method and specific results. Written practices stating a single 70 percent pass mark, or a single 80 percent, have described a grading scheme the standard does not contain, and every certificate issued under it is questionable.

Administration rules belong in the same section. Examinations shall not be self-administered and shall not be administered by a person the candidate supervises. In-house examination questions require Level III approval before use. A Level III who wrote the questions, sat the specific examination and signed off the result produced three findings from one afternoon — one reason firms route Level III examination and question-bank approval through ASNT Level III consulting services rather than keeping every signature inside the reporting line.

sections.heading: Vision: the shortest clause and the most frequent lapse
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A (2020) sets near-vision acuity at a minimum of Jaeger Number 2, or equivalent type and size letter, read at the distance designated on the chart and not less than 12 in. (30.5 cm), with an Ortho-Rater minimum of 8 or a similar test pattern accepted as an alternative. That examination is administered annually. Color contrast differentiation demonstrates the capability of distinguishing and differentiating among the colors or shades of gray used in the method, at initial certification and at five-year intervals afterwards.

Write both intervals, both acceptance criteria, and the role authorized to administer the test. State whether corrected vision is acceptable and require the record to note the correction. Two intervals running on two different clocks is precisely why this clause lapses: the annual near-vision date and the five-year color date drift apart, and the file ends up with one current and one expired.

A vision record dated fourteen months before the audit is a finding an auditor writes in under a minute, and it is the most common expired-record finding in NDT programs. The control that closes it is a calendar attached to the certification file rather than to a technician's memory — one tickler per technician, per test, with the next due date on the certificate cover sheet where the reviewer sees it.

sections.heading: Certification, recertification and interrupted service
paragraphs: The certification section names who signs the certificate, what the certificate shows, and how long it runs. SNT-TC-1A (2020) sets a recommended maximum recertification interval of five years for all levels, measured from the date the certifying authority signs the certification record. Earlier editions carried different intervals for Level I and II, so the written practice has to name the edition it invokes. A document that says "per SNT-TC-1A" with no year forces the auditor to pick an edition, and the auditor picks the one that produces the finding.

SNT-TC-1A permits recertification on evidence of continuing satisfactory technical performance, or by reexamination in whichever portions the Level III deems necessary. Choose one route, write it, and build the evidence that route requires. "Continuing satisfactory performance" is not a signature on a renewal form — it is the documented technical performance evaluation SNT-TC-1A calls for, in which the Level III periodically evaluates and records the performance of Level I and II personnel. Firms that select the evidence route and never run the evaluations have selected a route they cannot walk.

Interrupted service and termination need explicit thresholds. SNT-TC-1A leaves the interruption period to the employer, so the written practice states how many consecutive months away from the method triggers reexamination and which portions are reexamined. Termination carries more weight than most firms expect: an employer-based certificate holds only while the employment relationship holds, so a departing technician arrives elsewhere uncertified in your program's terms and a returning one needs a reinstatement route the document has already defined.

sections.heading: Designating the Level III: the signature holding the document up
paragraphs: The written practice names the certifying authority. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer's Level III can be qualified by the employer's own examination or hold ASNT NDT Level III certification, and the document states which route this company accepts, names the individual, and lists the methods that individual is qualified in. That method list is load-bearing. A Level III certified in UT and MT cannot approve a radiographic procedure or certify an RT Level II, and an auditor cross-referencing certificates against procedure approvals finds that mismatch inside an hour.

SNT-TC-1A's qualification routes for Level III run through a four-year engineering or science degree plus one additional year beyond Level II requirements, two years of engineering or science study plus two additional years, or four years beyond Level II in work comparable to Level II in the applicable method. ASNT's own NDT Level III scheme sets parallel eligibility — 12 months (252 days) of NDT experience with a four-year degree, 24 months (504 days) with two years of study, 48 months (1,008 days) with no college — and requires the NDT Basic examination plus at least one Method examination. The route your written practice invokes is the route your records must evidence; the ASNT scheme is set out in full on the ASNT certification page.

Name the deputy. A written practice with exactly one named Level III and no alternate stops functioning the day that person gives notice, and every certificate signed afterwards is unsupported. Companies that name a contracted Level III in the document alongside the staff Level III keep signing authority through a resignation without amending anything — the calculus is worked through in the outsourced versus in-house Level III comparison.

sections.heading: Approval, revision control and the records that prove it
paragraphs: The document carries an approval page with the employer's signature, the Level III's signature, a revision number and a revision date. Auditors check that the copy in the quality system matches the copy in the technician's binder, and that the revision history explains every difference between them. Uncontrolled copies circulating with a superseded method list produce a document-control finding before anyone opens a certification file.

The records section states what is retained, for how long, and where. At minimum: the training record with content and hours, the experience record by method, every examination paper and answer sheet with the grader's marks, the vision records, the technical performance evaluations, and the signed certification record. Examination papers are the record discarded most often, usually because the grade was transcribed to a summary sheet and the paper looked redundant. Their absence converts a compliant certification into an unverifiable one, and unverifiable is the same as absent in an audit report.

Set the review cycle in writing. A practice reviewed once at issue and never again drifts away from actual practice inside two years, and that drift produces the most common audit finding there is — catalogued alongside the other six in the NDT audit findings ranking. Firms that want the gap found before an auditor finds it run an NDT program audit gap assessment against the document and the records together, because neither one on its own shows where they disagree.

faq.q: How long does it take to produce a written practice?
faq.a: The drafting is short. The slow parts are the inputs: an accurate method list, current Level III certificates with the methods named, existing training and experience records to reconcile against, and a decision on the recertification route. Firms with those in hand move quickly. Firms discovering that half their experience records say "time employed" spend the time rebuilding records, not writing text.

faq.q: Does the written practice have to name a specific edition of SNT-TC-1A?
faq.a: Yes, and it is one of the cheapest findings to avoid. Editions differ on recertification intervals and vision clauses, so a document citing "SNT-TC-1A" with no year leaves the auditor to choose which edition to measure you against. Name the edition, and re-verify the clauses you rely on whenever you move to a newer one.

faq.q: Can one written practice cover multiple sites?
faq.a: One document can cover multiple sites when the method scope, record forms and certifying authority are common across them. Where sites run different methods or report to different Level IIIs, the document needs a site-by-method matrix showing who certifies what, where. A single practice with a single named Level III covering three sites in three states fails on availability long before it fails on paper.

faq.q: Does a written practice cover API 510, 570 or 653 inspectors?
faq.a: No. API 510, 570 and 653 are individual certifications administered by API against their own bodies of knowledge and renewal cycles, not employer-based certifications issued under a written practice. A written practice governs the NDT personnel performing UT, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET on the assets those inspectors are responsible for. Keep the two record sets separate. Atlantis does not deliver API 510, 570 or 653 training.

faq.q: Who approves revisions to the written practice?
faq.a: The same two signatures that approved the original: the employer and the employer's NDT Level III. Revisions follow the document control rules in your quality system — new revision number, new date, superseded copies withdrawn. Where the revision adds a method, the training records, examinations and certificates for that method are completed before work in it begins, not afterwards.

faq.q: What is the first thing an auditor asks for?
faq.a: The written practice itself, followed by the certification records for three or four named technicians whose reports the auditor has already pulled. That sequence is deliberate. The document sets the standard you promised, the files show whether you met it, and the released reports show whether the people who signed them were authorized to. Every finding in a typical NDT audit falls out of those three stacks.

title: Staff or Contract NDT Level III: The Method-Breadth Decision
description: Staff or contract NDT Level III, decomposed: method breadth, audit-week availability, continuity risk, and the sole-Level-III resignation failure mode.
h1: Outsourced vs In-House NDT Level III: What Each One Actually Covers
answer: A staff Level III gives you daily availability and owns the written practice. A contract Level III gives you method breadth one salaried person rarely holds and continuity that survives a resignation. Firms selling four or more methods run both: staff for volume, contract for the methods and audit weeks the staff Level III cannot cover.
expansion: An in-house Level III is present daily, owns the written practice, runs technical performance evaluations, and signs procedures without a scheduling call. That person holds certification in the methods on their own certificate — commonly two or three. A firm selling UT, PT, MT, RT, ET, phased array and TOFD has a signing gap in every method the staff Level III does not hold, and that gap is invisible until an auditor cross-references certificates against procedure approvals. A contract Level III is engaged for the methods the staff cannot cover, for audit weeks when a single person cannot be in two plants, and for the interval after a resignation when the employer-based certificates signed by the departed Level III still need a certifying authority. The failure mode is not cost. It is the day the sole Level III gives notice and every certificate in the file traces back to one signature.

facets.q: Can a contracted Level III be the certifying authority named in our written practice?
facets.a: Yes. SNT-TC-1A places responsibility for certification on the employer, and the employer's written practice designates the Level III who reviews and approves it. Nothing in that structure requires the designated Level III to be on payroll. The document names the individual, states the methods they are qualified in, and the employer retains responsibility for the certifications issued under that signature.

facets.q: How many methods does a staff NDT Level III actually hold?
facets.a: Two or three is the common range, because each additional method is a further ASNT Method examination on top of the NDT Basic. ASNT lists the Basic at $545 for members and $625 for nonmembers, with Method examinations at $525–$545 and $605–$625. Adding four methods to one person means four examinations, preparation time, and the months in between.

facets.q: What stops working the day our only Level III resigns?
facets.a: Three things stop at once: procedure and technique approval, new certifications, and recertifications falling due. Certificates already signed stay in the file, and the auditor asks who is now the certifying authority for them. An empty answer is a program-level finding rather than a personnel one, and the gap runs from the resignation date to the day a replacement certificate is verified.

facets.q: Does CP-189 change the outsourced versus in-house decision?
facets.a: It tightens it. Under ANSI/ASNT CP-189 the employer's Level III shall hold current ASNT NDT Level III certification in the method, verified by the employer at each five-year recertification, and CP-189 requires a certification procedure that cannot be relaxed to suit company convenience. Programs working to CP-189 — nuclear, defense, ASME Section III and NQA-1 scopes — contract more, not less.

facets.q: Is it a conflict for a staff Level III to examine his own technicians?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A prohibits self-administered examinations and examinations administered by a person the candidate supervises. A staff Level III certifying technicians he directs daily sits close to that line, and in-house examination questions require his approval before use as well. A contracted Level III administering the examinations removes the question and reads better in a client audit.

facets.q: What does a contract Level III cost compared with a salary?
facets.a: The two are structured differently, which is why the direct comparison misleads. A salary recurs regardless of workload and buys the methods on one certificate. A contract is scoped against defined coverage — named methods, named audit weeks, named deliverables — and Atlantis quotes it on request. The comparison worth running is coverage against coverage, not line item against line item.

sections.heading: The decision is method coverage, not headcount
paragraphs: Inspection firms frame this as a hiring question — one more salary line or a contractor invoice. That frame produces the wrong answer, because the constraint is not how many Level IIIs you employ. It is how many of the methods you sell carry a valid certifying authority. A Level III certificate names methods. Approve a procedure in a method your certificate does not name and the approval is void, the certifications issued under it are void, and every report released against it is exposed.

Run the count before running the comparison. List every method on your service menu, with phased array and TOFD as separate lines rather than folded into UT. List every method named on your staff Level III's certificate. The difference is your coverage gap, and the coverage gap is the entire decision. A firm with two methods and a two-method Level III has nothing to decide. A firm selling seven methods against a three-method certificate has four methods with no certifying authority and no visibility into it until an auditor asks.

Then add the second axis: time. A certifying authority who exists but is offshore during your audit week covers the methods and not the moment. ASNT Level III consulting engagements are scoped against both axes, because the two gaps have different fixes and firms that solve one and ignore the other take the finding anyway.

sections.heading: What a staff Level III actually covers
paragraphs: Presence, first. A Level III on payroll walks the floor, watches technique in practice rather than on paper, and catches the drift between what the written practice says and what the crew does. That is the highest-value function of the role and the one a contract arrangement delivers least well. The written practice finding that heads every audit list exists because nobody was watching the gap widen between the document and the shop.

Ownership, second. The staff Level III treats the output of written practice development as a living document, approves revisions when a method is added, runs the technical performance evaluations SNT-TC-1A calls for on Level I and II personnel, and signs certification records on a schedule tied to the certification file rather than to a project. Continuity of small decisions — a technique variance, a specimen question, an acceptance-criteria call — accumulates into a program a client can audit without surprises.

The constraint is arithmetic. One person holds one certificate, and that certificate names the methods that person passed examinations in. ASNT's NDT Level III scheme requires the NDT Basic examination plus at least one Method examination, with eligibility running through 12 months of NDT experience with a four-year degree, 24 months with two years of study, or 48 months with none. Every method beyond the first is a further examination, further preparation and further months, and the service menu rarely waits.

sections.heading: What a contract Level III actually covers
paragraphs: Method breadth on demand. A contracted Level III is selected against the method that needs signing, which means the gap closes in the methods where it exists rather than in the methods one employee happens to hold. Firms adding TOFD or phased array to a service menu close the certifying-authority gap the same week the equipment arrives, instead of waiting out an examination cycle while jobs are already booked.

Documented independence, second. SNT-TC-1A prohibits self-administered examinations and examinations administered by a candidate's subordinate, and requires Level III approval of in-house examination questions. A contracted Level III administering the examinations removes the question a client auditor would otherwise raise. The same logic drives NDT program audit gap assessment work outside the reporting line — a program reviewed by the person who wrote it produces a review nobody believes.

Elasticity, third. Contract coverage scales to the audit calendar rather than the payroll calendar. Two client audits and a class survey inside a fortnight need three certifying authorities in three places; a staff Level III supplies one and apologizes for the other two. Firms running offshore NDT consulting scopes hit this every mobilization season, when the audit calendar and the work calendar collide by design.

sections.heading: Audit week: availability is not the same as presence
paragraphs: Auditors do not ask whether you employ a Level III. They ask for the certifying authority to answer for the program — the written practice he approved, the examination questions he signed off, the technical performance evaluations bearing his name, the technique sheets carrying his approval. A staff Level III who is on a job in another state when the auditor arrives is a staff Level III who is not available, and the audit does not reschedule around him.

Build availability into the arrangement explicitly. Named audit-support days inside a contracted Level III scope produce a person in the room on the day, with the personnel files read in advance and the likely questions already worked. Firms that discover on the Tuesday morning that their Level III is unreachable until Friday take the finding, and the finding reads as a program-control weakness rather than a scheduling accident.

Both models fail identically when nobody has read the file. The value on audit day is not the certificate on the wall; it is the person who can explain why a Level II's specific examination question set matches the procedure the crew actually runs, and produce the graded paper that proves it. That preparation is scoped work with hours attached, not a phone call the night before.

sections.heading: The method-breadth gap most firms discover late
paragraphs: Here is the shape of it. A fabrication shop sells UT, PT, MT and RT, then adds phased array for a customer and TOFD eighteen months later because the same customer asked. The staff Level III holds UT, PT and MT. RT procedures were approved years ago by a Level III who has since left. Phased array and TOFD procedures were written by a senior Level II and approved by the staff Level III, who holds no certificate in either. Nothing failed. Nothing was flagged. Three of five methods have no valid certifying authority.

The consequence is retroactive, which is what makes it expensive. When the mismatch surfaces, the auditor does not limit the finding to the next job. Procedures approved without authority get re-approved, certifications issued under those procedures get reviewed, and the released reports behind them come under question. The corrective action plan runs backwards through the file, and the customer who asked for phased array is the customer reading the plan.

The fix is a matrix, maintained quarterly: methods sold down one axis, certifying authority and certificate expiry across the other, with the empty cells visible. Firms that keep it find the gap the week it opens. Firms that build it during a corrective action find it after the customer has.

sections.heading: Continuity: the sole-Level-III failure mode
paragraphs: Employer-based certification is valid only within the employment relationship. A technician's certificate is not portable, and the Level III's certifying authority departs with the Level III. When the sole Level III resigns, procedure approval, new certifications and recertifications falling due all stop on the same day. The gap runs from the resignation date to the day a replacement's certificate is verified and named in the written practice, and in a thin market that period is measured in months, not weeks. Firms in that position work through what to do when the NDT Level III resigns before they work through recruitment.

Certificates already in the file are the second problem. They remain valid documents, and the auditor asks who is now the certifying authority responsible for them. An empty answer is a program-level finding, not a personnel one, and it applies to every technician in the file rather than to one. Naming an alternate in the written practice is what prevents it, and interim NDT Level III coverage is written to fill that named-alternate slot from the first day rather than the first available date.

Recruitment alone is a plan with a hole in it. Replacing a multi-method Level III takes longer than replacing a Level II, the candidate pool is small, and the strongest candidates are already covering somebody else's methods. Firms treating recruitment as the whole answer carry an uncovered program through the entire search. Firms treating it as half — interim coverage running while recruitment runs — carry nothing.

sections.heading: The cost comparison nobody runs correctly
paragraphs: The comparison most firms run is a salary line against an hourly rate, and it answers a question nobody asked. For reference on the salary side, Glassdoor puts the US average for an ASNT NDT Level III at $98,569 with a middle band from $75,628 to $130,199; Salary.com reports $61,522 for the same title. That spread tells you the job title is applied inconsistently across the market more than it tells you what the function costs. Bands by level and region are broken out on the NDT Level III salary page.

The comparison worth running is coverage against coverage. A staff Level III covering three of seven methods delivers three-sevenths of your certifying authority for the full salary. The other four methods are uncovered at any price, and uncovered methods never appear on a budget line — they appear in an audit report, a corrective action plan, and occasionally a customer's decision to move the work.

Third-party costs sit on both sides of the comparison and cancel less than firms expect. ASNT lists the NDT Basic examination at $545 for members and $625 for nonmembers, Method examinations at $525–$545 and $605–$625, with retakes lower, and certification renewing on a five-year cycle. Those fees are identical whether the person is on payroll or contracted. What changes is who carries them, how many methods they buy, and whether the calendar allows the examination to be sat before the work arrives.

sections.heading: Client and code acceptance of a contracted Level III
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A places responsibility for certification on the employer, and the employer's written practice designates the Level III who reviews and approves it. Nothing in that structure requires the designated Level III to be an employee. The document names the individual, states the methods, and the employer retains responsibility for the certifications issued. Auditors check the designation and the method match; payroll status is not a criterion in the recommended practice.

ANSI/ASNT CP-189 raises the bar in a way that pushes the other direction. Under CP-189 the employer's Level III shall hold current ASNT NDT Level III certification in the method, and the employer verifies that certificate at each five-year recertification. CP-189 also requires a certification procedure rather than a written practice, and that procedure cannot be relaxed to suit company requirements. Nuclear, defense, ASME Section III and NQA-1 programs that invoke CP-189 make it harder, not easier, for one salaried person to cover every method sold.

Client and class specifications override both. Owner specifications add requirements the base standard never states, and some name approval routes explicitly. Read the specification before choosing the model — maritime NDT consulting and IACS service supplier approval scopes both begin with that read, because a society's approval decision turns partly on whether the certifying-authority arrangement is acceptable to the society.

sections.heading: The hybrid most multi-method firms end up running
paragraphs: The structure that survives contact with an audit is a split one: a staff Level III for the two or three highest-volume methods and daily floor presence, plus a contracted Level III named in the written practice for the remaining methods, the audit weeks, and independence on examinations. That covers the method gap and the continuity gap with a single document change, and it stops the firm choosing between presence and breadth when it needs both.

Write both into the written practice explicitly. Name the staff Level III with methods, name the contracted Level III with methods, and state which signature carries which approval. The document then survives a resignation without an amendment, because the alternate is already designated and already verified. Section-by-section guidance on that clause — and on the designation section generally — is in the written practice walkthrough.

Then test it before an auditor does. A gap assessment run against the method matrix, the current certificates and the signatures on last quarter's released reports finds uncovered methods in a day, and it finds them in the same seven patterns catalogued in the audit findings ranking. Firms that run it annually stop discovering coverage gaps during audits, which is the only point at which discovering one is expensive.

faq.q: How quickly can a contracted Level III be named in our written practice?
faq.a: The naming is a revision to the document: new revision number, the individual and their qualified methods added to the designation section, employer and Level III signatures, superseded copies withdrawn. The work ahead of it is verification — confirming the certificate is current in each method being named and that the methods actually match your service list. Firms with an accurate method matrix move immediately.

faq.q: Do our existing certificates stay valid if the Level III who signed them leaves?
faq.a: The certificates remain in the file as issued, and the certifications themselves were validly made at the time. What ends is the signing authority going forward. The auditor's question is who is now the responsible certifying authority for that population, and the written practice has to answer it. Naming an alternate before the departure is what keeps the answer short.

faq.q: Can we run a staff Level III and a contracted Level III at the same time?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the common arrangement in firms selling four or more methods. The written practice names both, lists the methods each is qualified in, and states which signature carries which approval. The staff Level III holds the floor presence and the high-volume methods; the contracted Level III holds the balance, the audit-week cover and the examination independence.

faq.q: Does a contracted Level III satisfy an IACS service supplier approval?
faq.a: Class societies assess the arrangement, not the employment contract — whether a named certifying authority is qualified in the methods the firm offers, whether the written practice designates them, and whether the records support it. Several societies add their own requirements on top. Read the society's rules for your approval category first, because they set the bar the arrangement has to clear.

faq.q: How many audit-support days should a contract include?
faq.a: Count your audit calendar rather than guessing: client audits, class surveys, accreditation visits and internal audits, then add preparation days ahead of each. Firms that scope one day per audit find the Level III arriving cold. Firms that scope a preparation day plus the audit day get someone who has already read the files the auditor will pull.

faq.q: What is the first sign a firm has outgrown a single staff Level III?
faq.a: A procedure waiting on an approval. When a new technique, a new method or a customer-specific variance sits in a queue because the only person who can sign it is elsewhere or uncertified in that method, the coverage model has already broken. The audit finding follows later; the delay is the early warning, and it is measurable in your own job records.

title: The Seven NDT Audit Findings Auditors Write Most, and the Fix
description: The seven NDT program audit findings written most often, ranked — written practice drift, lapsed vision tests, expired certs — with the fix for each one.
h1: The Most Common NDT Program Audit Findings, Ranked, With the Fix for Each
answer: The most common NDT audit finding is a written practice that no longer describes what the shop does. Behind it: training records missing hours, vision tests past their annual date, certifications expired against the five-year interval, examination papers discarded, a Level III signing methods they hold no certificate in, and testing performed by uncertified personnel.
expansion: Audit findings in NDT programs cluster into a short list because they all trace to the same two documents: the written practice and the certification file. The written practice promises hours, intervals, grading rules and signing authority. The file either evidences those promises or it does not. Auditors work the gap in a fixed order — read the practice, pull three or four personnel files, check dates against the promised intervals, then compare signatures on released reports against the certificates behind them. Training records missing the hour breakdown, vision examinations dated more than twelve months back, certificates past the five-year recertification interval, discarded examination papers, a Level III approving a method they hold no certificate in, and a technician working under no valid certificate at all are what that sequence turns up. Each has a documented fix, and every one of them is cheaper to close before the auditor arrives.
source: Requirements cited from ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2020) — Written Practice, Examinations, Certification, Technical Performance Evaluation, Interrupted Service and Records — and from ANSI/ASNT CP-189 on employer Level III certification and recertification. Audit-conduct observations from ASNT's published guidance on NDT audits and from PRI/Nadcap AC7114 audit criteria for aerospace NDT programs. ASNT NDT Level III examination structure and fees from certification.asnt.org, retrieved August 2026.

table.note: Ranking reflects the recurrence pattern reported across employer-based NDT programs working to SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 and the audit criteria applied under PRI/Nadcap AC7114. Findings 1 through 5 are documentation failures. Findings 6 and 7 reach the product and are the two most likely to be written as major.

facets.q: What is the single most common NDT audit finding?
facets.a: A written practice that no longer describes actual practice. It sits at the top because it is generative: once the document and the shop diverge, every downstream record is measured against a promise the company stopped keeping. Methods added without a revision, hour figures nobody applies, and a named Level III who left two years ago are the three most common forms it takes.

facets.q: Why do lapsed vision tests keep appearing as findings?
facets.a: Because two clocks run at different speeds. SNT-TC-1A (2020) requires near-vision acuity examined annually and color contrast differentiation at initial certification and five-year intervals afterwards. Firms track one and drift on the other, and the file ends up with a current color record beside a fourteen-month-old near-vision form. Both dates belong on the certification cover sheet where a reviewer sees them.

facets.q: Can a Level III certify personnel in a method they are not certified in?
facets.a: No. The Level III is designated in the written practice for named methods, and the designation is what an auditor cross-references against procedure approvals and certification records. Under ANSI/ASNT CP-189 the requirement is explicit: the employer's Level III shall hold current ASNT NDT Level III certification in the method, verified at each five-year recertification. Signatures outside the named methods are void.

facets.q: Do we have to keep the actual examination papers?
facets.a: Yes. A transcribed grade on a summary sheet evidences that someone recorded a number, not that the candidate passed a compliant examination. Auditors ask for the graded general and specific papers, the answer key, and the practical checkpoint sheet showing what was evaluated. Without them the certification is unverifiable, and unverifiable reads the same as absent in a finding.

facets.q: What is the difference between a major and a minor finding?
facets.a: A minor finding is a documentation gap with no demonstrated effect on product. A major finding indicates the program failed in a way that could reach the product — testing performed by uncertified personnel, or approvals signed without authority — and it can fail the audit outright. Minors accumulate: several of the same type in one file get rewritten as one major.

facets.q: Does SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 apply to our program?
facets.a: The code, customer specification or accreditation scheme you work to names one. ASME Section V accepts both. SNT-TC-1A predominates in oil and gas, petrochemical, general manufacturing and structural steel; CP-189 is invoked in nuclear, defense and critical infrastructure work under ASME Section III and NQA-1. CP-189 states requirements rather than recommendations and cannot be relaxed to suit company preference.

sections.heading: Why the ranking looks the same in every shop
paragraphs: Findings cluster because they all trace to the same two artifacts: the written practice and the certification file. The document promises hours, intervals, grading rules and signing authority. The file either evidences those promises or it does not. Everything an auditor writes is a statement about the distance between them, which is why programs in aerospace, refining and shipyard work throw up the same seven items in roughly the same order despite working to different codes.

The sequence auditors follow is stable enough to rehearse. Read the written practice and note what it committed to. Pull three or four personnel files, weighted toward technicians whose reports are already in the sample. Check every date in those files against the intervals the document promised. Then compare the signatures on released reports against the certificates behind them, and the procedure approvals against the Level III's method list. ASNT's own guidance on NDT audits describes the same pattern: verify the procedure aligns with customer requirements, then verify the practice is being followed and documented.

That order matters for preparation. Fixing records without fixing the document leaves the promise intact and the gap open. Fixing the document without fixing records creates a fresh discrepancy between a current revision and a historical file. Programs that close findings permanently work both together, which is what an NDT program audit gap assessment is scoped to do.

sections.heading: Finding 1: the written practice no longer describes actual practice
paragraphs: This heads every list because it generates the others. A written practice is a set of commitments — these methods, these hours, this grading rule, this interval, this certifying authority — and once the shop moves and the document does not, every record in the file gets measured against a standard the company stopped applying. The three common forms are a method added without a revision, hour figures nobody applies in practice, and a named Level III who left the company two years ago.

Auditors find it in the first thirty minutes without opening a personnel file. The method list in the document is compared against last quarter's job files. A phased array report with no phased array in the scope section is the finding, and it arrives before any question about training records. The same comparison works on the codes cited: a document referencing a superseded edition while the crew works to the current one is the same failure in a different clause.

The fix is a reconciliation and a cycle. Reconcile the document against the current service menu, the current certificates and the record forms actually in use, then set a review cycle with a named owner and a date. Section-by-section guidance on what each clause has to state is in the written practice walkthrough, and firms rebuilding the document rather than patching it run written practice development against their own records instead of a template carrying somebody else's method list.

sections.heading: Finding 2: training records that record attendance, not hours
paragraphs: The written practice states training hours by method and level. SNT-TC-1A offers Table 6.3.1A for the employer to consider — 40 organized training hours and 210 experience hours in the method for UT Level I, a further 40 training hours and 630 cumulative experience hours at Level II — and whatever figures the employer adopts become the number the file has to evidence. What the file usually holds instead is a certificate saying a course was completed and a sign-in sheet saying somebody attended.

Auditors ask a specific question: show me the hours. A course completion certificate with no syllabus, no hour breakdown by topic and no instructor credentials answers none of it. The same problem appears on the experience side, where "employed since 2023" is offered as evidence of hours in the method. Employment is not experience, and an auditor who has seen the substitution once looks for it everywhere in the file.

Rebuild the record format rather than chasing missing paperwork. A compliant training record carries the syllabus, hours allocated by topic, the instructor's qualification, the dates, and a signed completion. A compliant experience record carries job type, method, hours and a supervising signature. Classroom hours delivered through corporate NDT training produce the first; the second has to be captured on the job, on a form designed before it is needed. Method-by-method hour figures are broken out in the NDT training hours guide.

sections.heading: Finding 3: vision examinations past their annual date
paragraphs: This is the fastest finding an auditor writes and the one that recurs most. SNT-TC-1A (2020) requires near-vision acuity permitting the candidate to read a minimum of Jaeger Number 2 or equivalent at the distance designated on the chart and not less than 12 in. (30.5 cm), with an Ortho-Rater minimum of 8 accepted as an alternative, examined annually. Color contrast differentiation demonstrates the ability to distinguish the colors or shades of gray used in the method, at initial certification and at five-year intervals afterwards.

Two intervals on two clocks is what breaks it. Firms track the five-year color date with the certification cycle and let the annual near-vision date float, so the file ends up with a current color record beside a near-vision form dated fourteen months back. The auditor reads one date and writes the finding. There is nothing to argue about, which is why it appears in reports that otherwise find little.

The control is a calendar attached to the certification file rather than to the technician. Put the next-due date for both examinations on the certificate cover sheet where the reviewer sees it, run a lookahead monthly, and name the role authorized to administer the test in the written practice so there is no ambiguity about who books it. Where a technician wears correction, the record notes the correction — an uncorrected result on a corrected technician is the same finding with an extra step.

sections.heading: Finding 4: certifications expired against the recertification interval
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A (2020) sets a recommended maximum recertification interval of five years for all levels, measured from the date the certifying authority signed the certification record. CP-189 works to the same five-year ceiling with tighter routes: Level I and II recertify by reexamination, or on documented experience with reexamination at least every ten years, and Level III recertification is the employer verifying that the individual's ASNT Level III certificate is current. The auditor checks a signature date against today's date, and arithmetic decides the outcome.

Two things push firms past the line. The first is a written practice citing "SNT-TC-1A" with no edition year, which leaves the interval ambiguous and lets the auditor choose. Earlier editions carried different intervals for Level I and II, so the document has to name the edition it invokes. The second is choosing the recertification route without building the evidence for it — SNT-TC-1A permits recertification on evidence of continuing satisfactory technical performance, but that evidence is the documented technical performance evaluation the Level III is required to perform periodically on Level I and II personnel. Firms that pick the evidence route and never run the evaluations have picked a route they cannot walk, and the finding lands on both clauses at once.

Run a ninety-day lookahead on every certificate in the file and treat the evaluation record as a standing obligation rather than a renewal formality. Where a technician has been out of the method, the interrupted service clause governs, and the written practice has to state the consecutive-month threshold and which examination portions are repeated. SNT-TC-1A leaves that number to the employer, so a document that never sets it has no defensible answer when the auditor asks.

sections.heading: Finding 5: examination records not retained
paragraphs: The certification record shows a composite grade. The auditor asks for the papers behind it, and the papers are gone — graded, transcribed to a summary sheet, and discarded because the sheet looked like the record. It is the single most avoidable finding on this list, and it converts a certification that was fully compliant when made into one nobody can verify.

What has to be retained is the whole set: the graded general examination, the graded specific examination, the answer keys, and the practical checkpoint sheet showing which checkpoints were evaluated on which specimen. SNT-TC-1A structures Level I and II qualification around those three written and practical parts, with the composite as the simple average and no individual part below 70 percent against a composite of at least 80. Without the papers, an auditor cannot confirm the composite was calculated the way the written practice describes, and cannot confirm the grading rule was applied at all.

Retention rules also cover who may have administered the examination. SNT-TC-1A states that examinations shall not be self-administered nor administered by a person the candidate supervises, and that in-house examination questions require Level III approval before use. The retained set has to show the administering signature and the approval trail. Firms that route Level III examination and question-bank approval through ASNT Level III consulting services keep the independence visible in the record rather than having to assert it in the meeting.

sections.heading: Finding 6: a Level III signing outside their qualified methods
paragraphs: This is where documentation findings start reaching the product. The Level III is designated in the written practice for named methods, and the designation is the basis of every procedure approval and certification record they sign. Approve a radiographic procedure on a certificate that names UT and MT and the approval is void, along with the certifications issued under it and the reports released against it. CP-189 states the requirement without room: the employer's Level III shall hold current ASNT NDT Level III certification in the method, verified by the employer at each five-year recertification.

Auditors find it by cross-reference, not by inspection. The Level III's certificate is placed beside the procedure approval sheets and the certification records, and the method columns are compared. It surfaces most often in firms that added a method for a customer — phased array or TOFD — and had the existing Level III approve a procedure a senior Level II wrote, because nobody treated the addition as a certifying-authority question.

The fix is structural. Build a method matrix with methods sold on one axis and certifying authority plus certificate expiry on the other, keep it current quarterly, and name an alternate Level III in the written practice for the methods the staff Level III does not hold. Firms weighing whether to close the gap by examination or by engagement work through it in the staff versus contract Level III comparison; the arithmetic usually favors naming an alternate, because each added method is a further ASNT Method examination and a further wait.

sections.heading: Finding 7: NDT performed by uncertified personnel
paragraphs: The most serious finding on the list, and the one most likely to be written as major, because it reaches the product directly. SNT-TC-1A requires personnel performing NDT to be qualified and certified under the employer's written practice. A report signed by someone with no current certificate in the method means the examination behind it has no qualification standing, and the customer holding that report has a problem the auditor has to record.

It rarely arrives as deliberate. The common route is an expired certificate nobody caught, a new hire working while paperwork is processed, a technician covering a method they hold at Level I under an instruction that calls for Level II interpretation, or a technician returning after a long absence with an interrupted service clause nobody applied. All four are administrative failures that produce a technical finding, which is why finding 7 usually appears in the same report as findings 3 and 4.

Gate the release, not the intent. Report release should require a current-certificate check against the method and level the report calls for, run as a control rather than a habit. Where a method has no valid certifying authority or no currently certified technician, work in that method stops until it does — that is a commercial decision made once, against a finding that costs far more. Firms that have already taken this finding usually restructure the whole control set, and a gap assessment covering the document, the files and last quarter's released reports is what tells them where the remaining exposure sits.

sections.heading: Major, minor, and what turns one into the other
paragraphs: Auditors classify findings by consequence. A minor finding is a documentation gap with no demonstrated effect on product — a missing hour breakdown, a form completed on the wrong revision. A major finding indicates the program failed in a way that could reach the product, and it can fail the audit outright. Findings 6 and 7 on this list start as major. Findings 1 through 5 start as minor and get promoted.

Promotion happens two ways. The first is accumulation: several minor findings of the same type across multiple files stop reading as isolated slips and start reading as a control that does not exist, which gets rewritten as one major against the system. The second is linkage. An expired vision record is minor on its own. An expired vision record on a technician who released a fluorescent penetrant report during the lapsed period links a documentation gap to a product decision, and the classification moves.

This is why closing findings one at a time under-performs. Corrective action that fixes the individual record leaves the control that allowed it, and the same finding returns at the next audit with an aggravating history. Corrective action that fixes the control — a lookahead calendar, a release gate, a review cycle with a named owner — closes the class rather than the instance, and auditors reading a repeat visit look specifically for which one you did.

sections.heading: The pre-audit pass that closes all seven
paragraphs: Every finding on this list is discoverable in a day by anyone willing to run the same sequence the auditor runs. Read the written practice and write down what it committed to: methods, hours, grading rule, intervals, named certifying authority with methods. Pull four personnel files spanning the methods you sell most. Check every date against the promised intervals. Compare the signatures on last quarter's released reports against the certificates behind them and the procedure approvals against the Level III's method list. What that produces is your finding list, before it is anyone else's.

Do it with someone outside the reporting line. A program reviewed by the person who wrote it returns the answers the writer already believes, and the two findings that reach the product — signing outside qualified methods and uncertified personnel — are the two an internal reviewer is least likely to write against their own signature. Independence is a requirement inside the standard for examinations, and it is a practical necessity for review. An NDT program audit gap assessment is scoped exactly this way, against the document and the records together.

Then fix the controls rather than the instances, and set the cycle. A lookahead calendar closes findings 3 and 4. A record format closes finding 2. A retention rule closes finding 5. A method matrix with a named alternate Level III closes finding 6, and a release gate closes finding 7. Finding 1 closes only with a review cycle and a named owner, which is why it sits at the top: it is the one that comes back the moment attention moves elsewhere. Firms with method coverage gaps behind findings 6 and 7 work through the coverage decision in the staff versus contract Level III comparison, because no calendar fixes a method nobody is certified to sign.

faq.q: How far back do auditors look in personnel files?
faq.a: To the origin of each certification in the file, because the question is whether the certification was validly made and has been validly maintained. That means the initial training and experience records, every examination since, every vision record in the interval, and every recertification decision. Files assembled to cover the last twelve months answer a question auditors are not asking.

faq.q: What do we do if a certification expired last month?
faq.a: Stop work in that method by that technician, complete the recertification against the route your written practice states, and record the lapse and the corrective action rather than backdating anything. Then check whether any report was released during the lapsed period — that is the exposure. Backdated certificates convert a recoverable minor finding into a records-integrity issue that no corrective action plan repairs.

faq.q: Can a finding be appealed?
faq.a: Auditors are expected to remain open to further evidence where a nonconformance is of questionable merit, and audit schemes provide an appeal route where the finding still stands. The appeal succeeds on evidence, not argument — the retained document the auditor did not see, the record that was misfiled. Appeals raised without new evidence consume the goodwill you need for the closure meeting.

faq.q: How many personnel files does an auditor pull?
faq.a: Enough to sample across the methods and levels your written practice covers, commonly three to five, weighted toward technicians whose reports are already in the audit sample. A finding in one file expands the sample. That expansion is the mechanism by which a single missing vision record becomes a review of every vision record in the program.

faq.q: Does an internal audit count as the fix?
faq.a: An internal audit finds the gap; it does not close it. Closure is evidenced by the changed control and the records that control has since produced — a lookahead calendar with completed cycles, a revised record format with files completed on it, a written practice revision with the Level III's signature. Auditors reading a corrective action plan look for the second half, and most plans stop at the first.

faq.q: Do these findings differ under CP-189 rather than SNT-TC-1A?
faq.a: The list is the same; the tolerance is narrower. CP-189 states requirements rather than recommendations and cannot be relaxed to suit company preference, requires a certification procedure rather than a written practice, and requires the employer's Level III to hold current ASNT NDT Level III certification in the method. Findings 1 and 6 are harder to argue against under CP-189 than under SNT-TC-1A.

title: Six Report Defects That Get an NDT Package Bounced Back
description: Missing procedure revision, unidentified calibration block, no certification reference: the six defects that get NDT reports returned, and the code behind each.
h1: The Rejected-Report Checklist: Six Fields Reviewers Look For First
answer: Inspection reports get rejected for six recurring defects: no procedure identification and revision, an unidentified calibration block or reference standard, no technician certification reference, a location description that cannot be re-found, acceptance criteria not stated, and results not tied to those criteria. ASME Section V makes most of these mandatory record content, not formatting preference.
expansion: A rejected inspection report costs more than the re-issue. The equipment stays isolated, the weld stays unaccepted, and the next survey window closes while a reviewer waits for a field that should have been on the form. ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section V treats report content as mandatory: Article 4 requires the procedure identification and revision, the instrument serial number, the search unit serial number, frequency and size, the beam angles, the couplant brand or type, and the cable type and length for every ultrasonic examination. Article 7 requires the examination personnel identity and, where the referencing code section calls for it, the qualification level, plus the date and time the examination was performed. Article 2 requires a radiograph review form listing each radiograph location and naming the representative who performed final acceptance. A report missing those fields does not fail on style. It fails the code.

Recurring-defect patterns from Atlantis NDT report review and programme audit work. Verify all clause numbers against the edition and addenda your contract invokes.
