facets.q: Which ASME Section V paragraph requires the procedure revision on the report?
facets.a: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4, paragraph T-493 requires procedure identification and revision to be recorded for each ultrasonic examination. Article 7, paragraph T-793 imposes the same requirement on magnetic particle examinations, alongside equipment type, current type, particle type, personnel identity and the date and time the examination was performed. The referencing code section can add fields on top.

facets.q: What has to appear on a UT report about the equipment used?
facets.a: ASME Section V paragraph T-492 requires the ultrasonic instrument identification including the manufacturer's serial number, the search unit identification including serial number, frequency and size, the beam angles used, the couplant brand name or type, and the search unit cable type and length. Omitting the serial numbers breaks traceability between the reading and a calibrated instrument.

facets.q: How should an indication location be written so it survives review?
facets.a: Give a fixed datum, the weld or component identification, a distance along a stated direction convention, and an offset from the weld centreline. ASME Section V paragraph T-491 requires the type, location and extent of every rejectable indication. A location that a second technician cannot reach with a tape measure and the report alone will not pass a repair-verification review.

facets.q: Does the report need to name the technician and the certification level?
facets.a: ASME Section V paragraph T-793 requires the examination personnel identity for magnetic particle work, plus the qualification level where the referencing code section calls for it. Beyond the code minimum, name, method, level, the written practice the certification was issued under, and the certification and vision expiry dates let a reviewer confirm currency without emailing the contractor.

facets.q: What does a radiographic package have to carry that a UT report does not?
facets.a: ASME Section V paragraph T-291 requires documented technique details: source or focal spot size, base material type and thickness, weld thickness and reinforcement, minimum source-to-object distance, source-side-to-film distance, film manufacturer and designation, number of films per cassette, and single or double wall exposure and viewing. Paragraph T-292 adds a radiograph review form naming the representative who performed final acceptance.

facets.q: Who is allowed to evaluate the results on an in-service inspection report?
facets.a: Under API 510 the examiner performs the nondestructive examination and does not evaluate results against the code unless specifically trained and authorised by the owner-operator. The inspector evaluates and accepts NDE results and makes the fitness-for-service recommendation. A report that records readings without identifying who evaluated them leaves that decision unattributed, and reviewers return it.

sections.heading: A Returned Report Is a Schedule Event, Not a Paperwork Event
paragraphs: The rejection email arrives three days after the crew demobilised. A reviewer at the client, the authorised inspector, or the attending surveyor has read the package and found a field missing. The examination itself was sound: the weld was scanned, the indication was sized, the call was correct. None of that survives, because the document carrying the result cannot be verified against anything. The report goes back, the technician who performed the work is on another job in another state, and the equipment stays isolated while a form gets corrected.

Nobody line-items this cost. It surfaces as a schedule slip on the turnaround, an extra attendance day on the class survey, or a second mobilisation that nobody quoted. The contractor absorbs the rework hours and the owner absorbs the downtime, so neither party's cost system attributes the loss to the report format. That accounting gap is precisely why the same handful of defects recurs across the industry, contract after contract, without anyone treating the format as the root cause.

Six defects recur: the procedure is not identified by number and revision, the calibration block has no identity, nothing ties the result to a certified person, the location cannot be found again, the acceptance criteria are absent, and the results are never compared to those criteria. Each has a named source in code. None requires judgment to fix. All six are template problems, which makes them solvable once rather than argued about on every job.

sections.heading: Defect One: The Procedure Has No Number and No Revision
paragraphs: ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section V, Article 4, paragraph T-493 requires the procedure identification and revision to be recorded for each ultrasonic examination. Article 7, paragraph T-793 opens with the same requirement for magnetic particle work. The revision is not decoration. It is the only thing connecting the result on the page to a specific, approved set of instructions covering scan plan, sensitivity, surface condition and evaluation level.

A reviewer who sees UT-01 with no revision letter cannot establish whether the technician worked to Revision 3, approved last quarter, or Revision 2, superseded because the calibration sequence changed. The reviewer has one defensible response, which is to return the report. Getting this right costs one field on the header block and a controlled procedure list that the [written practice](/consulting/written-practice-development) already obliges the contractor to maintain and a qualified [ASNT Level III](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) to approve.

sections.heading: Defect Two: The Calibration Block Has No Identity
paragraphs: ASME Section V paragraph T-492 requires the ultrasonic instrument identification including the manufacturer's serial number, the search unit identification including serial number, frequency and size, the beam angles used, the couplant brand name or type, and the search unit cable type and length. Contractors record the instrument and stop there. The reference standard the sensitivity was actually established on goes unnamed, and with it the entire basis of the measurement.

Sensitivity has no meaning apart from the reflector it was set on. A report stating 80% full screen height from a side-drilled hole is uninterpretable without the block identification, the material, the thickness, the hole diameter and depth, and the block's own calibration status. Record the block ID and its certificate reference alongside the instrument serials, and a reviewer can reproduce the setup two years later during a fitness-for-service assessment.

sections.heading: Defect Three: Nothing Ties the Result to a Certified Person
paragraphs: ASME Section V paragraph T-793 requires the examination personnel identity for magnetic particle examinations and, where the referencing code section calls for it, the qualification level. That is the code floor. The commercial floor sits higher, because the reviewer needs to establish that the named person held a current certification in the method, at the level the scope required, on the date the work was actually performed.

ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A places certification with the employer. The employer prepares the written practice, the employer's Level III approves it, and the certification record carries the printed legal name and signature of the designated Level III who verified the candidate's qualifications. A report that names a technician without pointing at that record leaves a reviewer holding a name and nothing else.

In-service work adds a second layer. Under API 510 the examiner performs the nondestructive examination and does not evaluate the results against the code unless specifically trained and authorised by the owner-operator, while the inspector evaluates and accepts the results and makes the fitness-for-service recommendation. Two roles, two names, two signature blocks. Collapsing them into one line reading Inspected By invites the exact question the report exists to answer.

sections.heading: Defect Four: The Location Cannot Be Found Again
paragraphs: Paragraph T-491 requires the type, location and extent of every rejectable indication, and directs that non-rejectable indications be recorded as the referencing code section specifies. Slag near the north end satisfies none of that. A location description passes when a second technician, holding only the report and a tape measure, can put a probe on the same square centimetre of metal on a different day.

That means a fixed datum, the weld or component identification, a distance along a stated direction convention, an offset from the weld centreline, and a sketch or model reference. Owners running a [digital twin](/digital-twins) of the asset get this for free, because the indication is pinned to a coordinate on the model rather than described in prose. Repair verification, remaining-life calculation and the next inspection interval all depend on returning to the same spot.

sections.heading: Defect Five: The Acceptance Criteria Are Not on the Page
paragraphs: A thickness reading without a criterion is a number. An indication length without a criterion is an observation. Neither is an inspection result, and a reviewer who has to go and find the governing clause before the report means anything will send it back rather than do the contractor's work for them. State the code, the edition, the clause and the table, quoted on the report itself, next to the result they govern.

Edition control matters as much as the clause number. The contract invokes a specific edition and addenda, and acceptance limits move between editions. A report citing a code without the year forces the reviewer to guess which set of limits was applied, and guessing is the one thing a quality record exists to eliminate. Print the edition and the addenda date in the header, and the ambiguity disappears permanently.

sections.heading: Defect Six: The Results Do Not Meet the Criteria on the Page
paragraphs: Stating the criteria in one section and the results in another leaves the comparison to the reader. Paragraph T-292 requires the radiograph review form to carry the evaluation and disposition of the materials or welds examined, the identification of the representative who performed final acceptance, and the date of that evaluation. The comparison is the deliverable, not an implication the reviewer is expected to draw unaided.

Build it as a per-indication row: indication identifier, type, location, measured dimension, the criterion limit that applies, the disposition, and the person who made the call. A reader scanning that table sees exactly how each judgment was reached and can audit any single line. A reader scanning a paragraph of prose followed by a bare ACCEPT stamp sees an assertion, and assertions get returned.

sections.heading: What a Compliant Report Carries, Front to Back
paragraphs: Header block: client, asset and component identification, work order, procedure number and revision, code and edition with the acceptance clause named, examination date and shift, location or drawing reference, and the surface condition and stage of manufacture or service. This block answers what was examined, under whose instructions, and against which limits. Populate it first and six of the common rejection triggers are already closed.

Technique block: instrument make, model and serial number, search unit or yoke or source details with serial numbers, couplant or consumable batch designations, calibration block or reference standard identification with its calibration status, beam angles or exposure parameters, cable type and length, and the lighting equipment where the method requires it. This block answers whether an independent party can reproduce the result.

Results and disposition block: the per-indication table, the acceptance decision against the stated criterion, the technician's name, level, certification reference and vision currency, the reviewer or Level III who evaluated the results, and the dated signatures of both. This block answers who is accountable for the call. Three blocks, populated every time, and the six defects have nowhere left to appear.

sections.heading: Format Is a Code Requirement, and Templates Beat Discipline
paragraphs: The argument that report layout is house style survives only until somebody reads the record paragraphs. ASME Section V does not describe a preferred appearance; it lists fields that shall be recorded. Article 2 mandates documented technique details and a radiograph review form. Article 4 mandates procedure identification and revision plus the equipment records. Article 6 mandates penetrant, remover, emulsifier and developer designations, the indication map, material and thickness, and the lighting equipment. Article 7 mandates personnel identity and the date and time.

Relying on technicians to remember a dozen mandatory fields at the end of a twelve-hour shift is a control that fails at exactly the moment it is needed. A structured capture form that refuses submission until every mandated field carries a value converts the code requirement into a property of the system. The same data record then drives the client's template, the internal quality file and the [ERP job record](/erp) without a second transcription, which is also where most of the [report turnaround time](/blog/ndt-inspection-report-turnaround-time) hides.

Contractors who have collected several rejections in a row have a systemic problem in the written practice, the procedure set, or the report template, usually all three at once. A structured [NDT programme audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) finds the missing fields against the codes the contracts actually invoke, before a client or a surveyor finds them. Owners sitting on the other side of this conversation should read the [contractor vetting checklist](/blog/choosing-an-ndt-service-provider-checklist) and ask for a sample report before award.

faq.q: Is NDT report format actually a code requirement or just a client preference?
faq.a: It is a requirement. ASME Section V lists fields that shall be recorded for each examination: procedure identification and revision, equipment and consumable identification, personnel identity, indication maps, material and thickness, lighting equipment, and the date the work was performed. The visual layout is free. The content is not, and a package missing mandated content fails the code regardless of how it looks.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to stop reports being returned?
faq.a: Rebuild the template so every code-mandated field is a required entry, then make submission impossible until all of them carry a value. That single change moves compliance out of a technician's memory at the end of a shift and into a property of the form itself, which is the only place a control of this kind survives a busy turnaround.

faq.q: Do the record requirements change between UT, RT, MT and PT?
faq.a: The principle holds and the fields differ. Article 2 requires documented radiographic technique details and a review form. Article 4 requires the instrument, search unit, beam angle, couplant and cable records. Article 6 requires penetrant, remover, emulsifier and developer designations plus material, thickness and lighting equipment. Article 7 requires equipment, current type, particle type, personnel identity and the date and time.

faq.q: Who signs an NDT report?
faq.a: The technician who performed the examination signs for the work, and the person who evaluated the results against the acceptance criteria signs for the disposition. Under API 510 those are two distinct roles, examiner and inspector, and collapsing them into a single signature block removes the accountability the record exists to create. Name both, with certification references and dates.

faq.q: How long should NDT records be retained?
faq.a: Retention is set by the referencing code and the contract. ASME requires the manufacturer to retain the radiographs and the records described in Article 2 until the Manufacturer's Data Report has been signed by the Inspector. Owner-operators running in-service programmes retain inspection records for the life of the asset. Write the retention period and the handover format into the purchase order.

title: Vetting an Inspection Contractor: 9 Documents to Demand
description: Certification currency, the written practice, calibration records, insurance and approvals: the nine documents that separate a real NDT programme from a paper one.
h1: The Asset Owner's Due-Diligence Checklist for NDT Contractors
answer: Ask for nine documents before awarding NDT work: the written practice, each technician's certification record with the Level III signature, current vision records, equipment calibration certificates with due dates, the examination procedures the scope invokes, certificates of insurance, third-party approvals held, the Level III's own qualification, and a sample report. Every document should arrive within one business day.
expansion: The difference between a functioning NDT programme and a paper one shows up in how fast the documents arrive. A contractor running a real programme keeps certification records, vision examinations, calibration certificates and controlled procedures in one system and produces them on request. A contractor selling bodies produces a scanned certificate, a promise, and a delay. ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A puts the burden on the employer: the employer writes the written practice, the employer's Level III approves it, and the certification record carries the printed name and signature of the Level III who verified the candidate's qualifications. That signature is the single highest-yield thing an asset owner can ask to see, because it identifies a named, qualified person who is accountable for every certification the contractor issues. If the contractor cannot name that person, the certifications behind the technicians on your site have no verifiable basis.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (written practice, employer certification records, Level III signature, annual near-vision verification); IACS Unified Requirement Z17 (approval of service suppliers, certificate of approval scope and limitations, personnel qualification and training); Nadcap OP 1111 accreditation length and Supplier Merit criteria; API 510 (examiner and inspector roles); ASME BPVC Section V (equipment and personnel records). Bid-evaluation practice from Atlantis NDT programme audit work.

Ask for the procedure list with revision numbers and dates, and compare it against your scope of work

table.note: Match the approval scheme to the asset. IACS UR Z17 covers class society approval of service suppliers for thickness measurement and in-water survey. Nadcap covers aerospace NDT processing. ISO/IEC 17025 covers laboratory competence. ISO 9001 covers the management system, not technical capability.

facets.q: Who is supposed to sign an NDT technician's certification record?
facets.a: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A places certification with the employer, and the certification record carries the printed legal name and signature of the designated Level III who verified the candidate's qualifications. Where the written practice names the certifying authority as a separate position, both signatures appear. Ask for the record, then ask who that Level III is and whether they are employed or contracted.

facets.q: How often does an NDT technician's vision have to be checked?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A calls for near-vision acuity to be verified annually, to Jaeger Number 1 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches, along with a colour contrast differentiation check on the interval the written practice sets. Ask for the dated record for each named technician mobilising to your site, not a blanket assurance covering the workforce.

facets.q: What third-party approvals actually mean something for NDT work?
facets.a: Match the approval to the asset. Class society service supplier approval under IACS UR Z17 covers thickness measurement and in-water survey work on ships. Nadcap covers aerospace NDT processing. ISO/IEC 17025 covers laboratory competence. ISO 9001 covers the management system, not technical capability. Verify every certificate number on the issuing body's own register rather than accepting the supplied PDF.

facets.q: How does a Nadcap audit cycle tell you about a supplier's performance?
facets.a: Nadcap accredits an initial audit for 12 months, then the following two reaccreditations for 12 months each. Extension to 18 months requires at least a second reaccreditation in the commodity with no non-sustaining corrective actions, no verification-of-corrective-action audits and no Type C auditee advisories. A 24-month interval requires two consecutive prior accreditations of at least 18 months. The interval itself is a performance signal.

facets.q: What insurance should an NDT contractor carry on an owner's site?
facets.a: Require a certificate of insurance naming your entity as additional insured, covering commercial general liability, automobile liability, workers' compensation and employer's liability, and professional liability or errors and omissions for the inspection opinion itself. Where radiography is in scope, confirm the policy does not exclude radioactive contamination. Check the certificate's effective dates against the campaign dates, not against the award date.

facets.q: Which single question separates a real programme from a paper one?
facets.a: Ask the contractor to produce, within one business day, the certification record and current vision record for three named technicians they intend to mobilise. A contractor with a live programme sends them from a system in minutes. A paper programme asks which technicians you mean, then goes quiet. Response time measures the system; the documents measure the people.

sections.heading: You Are Buying a Records System, Not a Crew
paragraphs: The asset owner selecting an inspection contractor is buying two things at once: technicians who can find flaws, and a records system that will still stand up when a regulator, an insurer or an opposing expert reads it four years from now. The first is straightforward to assess on site during a trial job. The second stays invisible until it fails, and it fails at the worst possible moment, with the scaffold down and the survey window closing.

Contractors understand this asymmetry. A bid gets won on day rate and crew availability, and the documentation deficit surfaces only when reports arrive incomplete, when a technician's certification turns out to have lapsed mid-campaign, or when a surveyor declines to accept thickness readings from a supplier who is not approved for the service. Each of those costs the owner equipment availability while costing the contractor nothing that appears on an invoice.

Nine documents, requested before award and produced within one business day, close most of that gap. The documents themselves matter. The response time matters more, because it measures whether an operating system exists or whether somebody is assembling a package in reaction to your email. Both signals arrive from a single request that takes ten minutes to send.

sections.heading: Document One: The Written Practice
paragraphs: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A places the burden of qualification and certification squarely on the employer. The employer prepares a written practice describing how its personnel are trained, examined, certified and recertified, and that document is kept on file and approved by the employer's Level III. Every technician certificate the contractor issues derives its authority from that one document, which makes it the first thing to read and the fastest thing to test.

Ask which edition the written practice follows, whether it has been revised since, and whether the Level III's signature appears on the approval page. Ask whether it states the recertification interval and the training and experience hours required per method and per level. A contractor who cannot produce the written practice inside a day is issuing certificates with nothing behind them, and a [written practice review](/consulting/written-practice-development) will establish that in an afternoon.

sections.heading: Documents Two and Three: Certification Records and Vision Currency
paragraphs: Request the certification record for each named technician being mobilised, not a company-wide statement of capability. The record should show the method, the level, the issue date, the expiry date, the written practice it was issued under, and the printed legal name and signature of the designated Level III who verified the candidate's qualifications. Where the written practice separates the Level III from the certifying authority, both signatures belong on the record.

Vision runs on its own clock and lapses independently of the certification. SNT-TC-1A calls for near-vision acuity verified annually, to Jaeger Number 1 or equivalent at not less than 12 inches, plus a colour contrast differentiation check on the interval the written practice sets. A lapsed vision record undermines the technician's ability to perform the examination regardless of what the certification card says, and it is a currency failure that routine audits find repeatedly.

sections.heading: Document Four: A Named, Qualified Level III
paragraphs: Behind every credible NDT programme is one named person with the technical authority to write and approve procedures, resolve interpretation disputes, and stand behind the certifications the company issues. Ask who that person is, which methods their qualification covers, and whether they are an employee or an external appointment. Both arrangements work in practice. What does not work is a programme where nobody in the organisation can name them without checking.

Test the answer rather than filing it. Put a scope-specific technical question to the Level III during bid clarification: how they would establish sensitivity on a particular geometry, or which acceptance table governs your service condition. A Level III who engages with the question is real. An [outsourced Level III arrangement](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) is entirely legitimate, provided the person is named in the written practice, contactable, and available when a dispute lands mid-shift.

sections.heading: Document Five: The Examination Procedures
paragraphs: Every method in the scope needs a written, revision-controlled procedure approved by the Level III and demonstrated where the referencing code requires demonstration. Ask for the procedure list with revision numbers and approval dates, then compare it line by line against the methods and configurations in your scope of work. A gap between the two is a contractor who intends to write the procedure after award, or to work without one and hope nobody asks.

The procedure set is also what makes the reports defensible downstream, because ASME Section V requires the procedure identification and revision to be recorded on the examination record itself. A contractor without controlled revisions cannot populate that field truthfully, which is the first of the [report defects that get packages returned](/blog/ndt-report-format-what-clients-reject) and the one that generates the most rework on a large campaign.

sections.heading: Document Six: Equipment Calibration Records
paragraphs: Request calibration certificates for the instruments, blocks and reference standards that will be used on your campaign, then check the serial numbers against the serial numbers that will appear on your reports. ASME Section V requires the instrument and search unit identification, including manufacturer's serial numbers, to be recorded on the examination record. The traceability chain either closes on paper or it does not, and it is faster to check before award than after rejection.

Check due dates against campaign dates rather than against the award date. A reference block certificate expiring mid-turnaround invalidates every reading taken after it lapses, and the discovery happens on review, after the unit is back in service. Ask what the contractor does when a calibration lapses mid-campaign. A real programme has a documented answer involving recall, notification and re-examination of affected work.

sections.heading: Documents Seven and Eight: Insurance and Third-Party Approvals
paragraphs: Require a certificate of insurance naming your entity as additional insured, covering commercial general liability, automobile liability, workers' compensation and employer's liability, and professional liability or errors and omissions for the inspection opinion itself. Where radiography is in scope, confirm the policy does not exclude radioactive contamination. Match the effective dates to the campaign dates, and re-request the certificate if the campaign extends past expiry.

Approvals must match the asset. IACS Unified Requirement Z17 governs class society approval of service suppliers performing thickness measurement and in-water survey work on ships. The society issues a certificate of approval stating the type and scope of services and any limitations or restrictions, including equipment types where that is a constraint, and it holds the supplier responsible for qualifying and training its personnel to a recognised standard. Confirm the [service supplier approval](/consulting/iacs-service-supplier-approval) covers your service and the society attending your survey.

Nadcap accreditation applies to aerospace NDT processing and carries a readable signal in its own audit cycle. The initial audit accredits for 12 months, and the following two reaccreditations run 12 months each. Extension to 18 months requires no non-sustaining corrective actions, no verification-of-corrective-action audits and no Type C auditee advisories since the previous audit. A 24-month interval requires two consecutive prior accreditations of at least 18 months, which means a supplier holding one has an unusually clean history.

sections.heading: Document Nine: A Sample Report From Live Work
paragraphs: Ask for a redacted report from recent work in your industry, not a marketing sample built for a brochure. Read it the way a reviewer would read it. Does it carry the procedure number and revision? The instrument and calibration block serial numbers? The technician's name, level and certification reference? The acceptance criteria with code, edition and clause? A per-indication comparison against those criteria, signed and dated by whoever made the call?

A contractor whose standard output carries all of that will not generate rejections on your account. A contractor whose sample is a photograph and a paragraph of narrative will generate them from the first campaign onward, and every one of those rejections costs you equipment availability while costing them only rework hours. The sample report is the cheapest predictive test in the entire evaluation.

sections.heading: The Questions That Separate a Programme From a Paperwork Exercise
paragraphs: Four questions do most of the work. Who is your Level III and which methods does their qualification cover? Which edition of SNT-TC-1A is your written practice written to, and when was it last revised? What happens when a technician's certification or vision record lapses mid-campaign? Show me the certification and vision records for three named technicians you intend to mobilise, by tomorrow morning.

Response time is the measurement, not the content of the answers. A contractor running a live records system answers all four within minutes, pulling from a database that already exists because their own quality system depends on it. A contractor running a paperwork exercise asks which technicians you mean, then goes quiet for a week. Nothing else in a bid evaluation yields that much signal for that little effort.

Owners who want the evaluation done independently, or who inherited a contractor and need to know what they actually have, use a structured [NDT programme audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) against the codes their contracts invoke. Vessel owners with class attendance coming should also confirm [UTM operator qualification and class approval](/consulting/utm-operator-qualification-class-approval) before the survey window opens. [Send the scope](/contact) and the gaps come back as a document, not an opinion.

faq.q: Does ISO 9001 certification mean an NDT contractor is technically competent?
faq.a: No. ISO 9001 certifies the management system, not the technical capability of the inspection work. Technical competence comes from the written practice, the Level III standing behind it, the qualified and revision-controlled procedures, the personnel certification records, and any method-specific third-party approval such as class society service supplier approval, Nadcap accreditation or ISO/IEC 17025 laboratory accreditation.

faq.q: Can a contractor use a subcontracted Level III?
faq.a: Yes, and many competent programmes do. The requirement is that the Level III is named in the written practice, qualified in the methods being certified, and reachable when an interpretation dispute happens on shift. Ask for the name, the qualification scope and the response commitment. An unnamed or unreachable Level III is a programme with no technical authority behind it.

faq.q: What should be in the scope of work rather than left to the contractor?
faq.a: The codes and editions governing acceptance, the methods and coverage required, the report format and per-stage delivery deadlines, the certification levels required for interpretation, and the insurance and approval requirements. Leaving any of these to the contractor's discretion produces a bid that is cheap for a reason, and the reason surfaces during review rather than during evaluation.

faq.q: How do I verify a certificate a contractor sends me?
faq.a: Check the number on the issuing body's own register rather than trusting the PDF. Class societies publish approved service supplier lists. Nadcap accreditation is verifiable through the eAuditNet system. ASNT verifies its own Level III certifications. A certificate that cannot be verified at source is a document, not an approval, and it carries exactly the weight of the paper it is printed on.

faq.q: Is the lowest bid ever the right choice for inspection work?
faq.a: When two contractors both clear the nine-document check, price decides and the lowest bid wins on merit. When one clears it and one does not, the difference in bid price is a transfer of risk rather than a saving, because a rejected report costs the owner equipment availability while costing the contractor only rework hours nobody bills.

title: Eight Handoffs Between Probe and PDF: NDT Report Turnaround
description: Field capture, transcription, Level III review, client format, invoice: where NDT report turnaround goes, and what the equipment downtime costs while it sits.
h1: Where NDT Report Turnaround Actually Goes, Stage by Stage
answer: NDT report turnaround breaks into eight stages: field capture, data offload, transcription, technician review, Level III or Level II review, client-format assembly, approval signature, and issue. Transcription and review consume the bulk of it, and both are queueing time rather than work time. Field capture on a structured digital form collapses transcription to zero and cuts the cycle sharply.
expansion: The inspection is the short part. A technician shoots a weld, gauges a shell course or scans a nozzle in minutes, then the data enters a paper-and-transcription pipeline that runs for days. Every hour in that pipeline is an hour the asset stays isolated, the scaffold stays rented and the turnaround crew stands by. The cost of the delay lands on the client, not the contractor, which is why report turnaround almost never improves on its own, because the party holding the pen does not hold the meter. The cycle has eight identifiable stages, and the two longest are transcription from field notes into a template and the wait for a qualified reviewer to sign. Neither is examination work. Both disappear when field capture is structured at source and review is queued electronically rather than by email. That is a systems problem with a systems fix.
source: Cycle decomposition from Atlantis NDT reporting deployments and programme audit work. Role separation between examiner and inspector per API 510. Mandatory record content per ASME BPVC Section V Articles 2, 4, 6 and 7. Day figures in the table are contract targets recommended for a scope of work, not survey data; set and measure them against your own campaigns.

table.note: Day figures are contract targets to write into a scope of work, not survey results. Set them per stage rather than as one end-to-end number, so a late report can be traced to the stage that slipped instead of triggering an argument about the total.

facets.q: Which stage of the report cycle actually takes the longest?
facets.a: Two stages dominate: transcription of field notes into the report template, and the wait for a qualified reviewer to evaluate and sign. Neither is examination work. Both are queue time created by handoffs between people and formats. Removing transcription entirely and putting review into an electronic queue collapses the majority of the elapsed time without changing how the inspection is performed.

facets.q: What does a slow inspection report cost the asset owner?
facets.a: The asset stays isolated, the blind stays in, the scaffold stays rented and the turnaround crew stands by while a document is typed. The delay cost lands on the owner, while the rework cost lands on the contractor, so neither party's ledger shows the full number. Writing per-stage turnaround targets into the scope of work puts the cost back where it can be managed.

facets.q: Can a preliminary result be issued before the full report?
facets.a: Split the deliverable. A field advisory carrying the indication type, location, extent and the technician's preliminary call reaches the owner the same shift and lets repair planning start. The formal report follows once the qualified reviewer has evaluated and signed. Write both into the scope with separate deadlines, and state clearly that the advisory is preliminary and carries no acceptance decision.

facets.q: Why does re-keying data into the client's template take so long?
facets.a: Because it is a second full transcription performed by someone who did not do the inspection. Each owner runs its own template, its own portal and its own field names, so a contractor serving six owners maintains six output formats by hand. One structured data record driving multiple output templates removes the stage completely and eliminates the transcription errors that trigger rejections.

facets.q: How should turnaround be written into a scope of work?
facets.a: Set a target per stage rather than one end-to-end figure. Name the deadline for the field advisory, for the reviewed draft, and for the issued signed report, each measured from the end of the shift the data was captured. A per-stage clock lets a late report be traced to the stage that slipped instead of triggering an argument about the total.

facets.q: Does faster reporting increase the rejection rate?
facets.a: The opposite. Rejections come from missing mandatory fields, procedure revision, instrument serial number, calibration reference, personnel identity and acceptance criteria, and those are exactly the fields a structured capture form makes mandatory at the point of entry. Speed and completeness rise together when the form enforces the code requirements instead of relying on a technician remembering them after a long shift.

sections.heading: The Inspection Is the Short Part
paragraphs: A shear wave scan on a nozzle weld takes twenty minutes. A shell course of thickness readings takes an afternoon. A set of radiographs on a pipe spool takes a shift. Then the data leaves the site and enters a pipeline of transcription, review, formatting and signature that runs for days, and the asset that was isolated for the examination stays isolated for the paperwork that follows it.

The asymmetry is the whole problem. The technical work is measured in hours and the administrative work is measured in days, and the second number is the one that determines when the unit comes back online. Owners negotiate hard on the first number and accept whatever happens on the second, which is how a twenty-minute scan turns into a week of unavailability on a critical piece of plant.

Report turnaround is a systems property, not a matter of contractor diligence. It decomposes into eight identifiable stages, each with a different cause of delay and a different fix. Naming the stages is what makes the total negotiable, because a single end-to-end number can only be argued about after the fact, while a per-stage clock can be managed while the campaign is still running.

sections.heading: Stages One and Two: Field Capture and Data Offload
paragraphs: Capture is where the cycle is won or lost. A technician recording readings on a paper sheet or a phone photograph creates a record that somebody else has to interpret later. A technician entering readings into a structured form creates the report's data record directly, at the moment of examination, with the instrument settings and surface conditions attached. The difference in effort at the point of capture is negligible. The difference downstream is the entire transcription stage.

Offload is pure logistics: notes, thermal prints, radiographic files or encoded scan data moving from a site with no connectivity to an office with a template. Contractors lose a day here waiting for a crew to return from a remote location, or for a technician to email files from a hotel at the end of a hitch. Offline-capable capture that syncs automatically when signal returns removes the stage without changing anything about the field routine.

sections.heading: Stage Three: Transcription, the Largest Single Loss
paragraphs: Transcription is a person retyping field notes into a report template. It creates no information that did not already exist. It consumes hours per report, it scales linearly with volume, and it introduces the transcription errors that later cause rejections. On a campaign producing forty reports it becomes the constraint on the entire delivery, and it is performed by somebody who was not present at the examination and cannot verify what they are copying.

This stage disappears completely when capture and reporting share one data record. The technician's entries in the field are the report's contents, and the template becomes a rendering of that record rather than a document somebody types from scratch. Contractors who make that change once stop paying for the stage on every job afterwards, and the [ERP job record](/erp) updates from the same data without a third round of entry.

sections.heading: Stages Four and Five: Technician Review and Qualified Review
paragraphs: Self-review is fast and worth its cost: the examiner checks the record against the procedure for completeness before it moves anywhere. The failure mode is that it happens from memory at the end of a shift. Validation rules that block submission until the procedure revision, instrument serial numbers, calibration reference, personnel identity and acceptance criteria all carry values convert this from a habit into a property of the form itself.

Qualified review is the second large loss, and it is queue time rather than work time. A Level III or a certified Level II evaluating indications and dispositions needs perhaps thirty minutes per report, and receives it three days after the shift, buried in an email thread, without the scan data attached. The evaluation itself is quick. The waiting, the chasing and the re-sending of missing attachments are what consume the calendar.

Under API 510 the distinction is formal: the examiner performs the examination, while the inspector evaluates and accepts the results and makes the fitness-for-service recommendation. That handoff has to happen and it has to be documented. Putting it in an electronic queue, with the evidence attached and the reviewer notified on submission, converts a three-day wait into a same-day one without touching the technical content of the decision.

sections.heading: Stage Six: Re-Keying Into the Client's Template
paragraphs: Every asset owner runs its own report template, its own field names and often its own document portal. A contractor serving six owners maintains six output formats by hand, which means a second full transcription of data that has already been transcribed once. The person doing it did not perform the inspection and is copying between two documents, neither of which they are qualified to technically verify.

One structured data record driving multiple output templates eliminates the stage entirely. The owner receives their format, the contractor keeps one source of truth, and the copy errors that trigger rejections stop being generated at source. Owners can accelerate this from their side by supplying the template specification at award rather than at first delivery, which is when most contractors discover it exists.

sections.heading: Stages Seven and Eight: Signature and Distribution
paragraphs: The approval signature is a small stage with enormous variance. A report sits complete and reviewed, waiting for one authorised person to be at a desk with a printer and a scanner. Electronic signature bound to the signatory's certification record removes the geography from the problem and produces a stronger evidentiary record than a scanned squiggle, because the signature carries the certification reference and the timestamp with it.

Distribution should be automatic on approval: the client contact, the authorised inspector, the owner's records system and the contractor's own quality file all receive the same issued document at the same moment. Emailing a PDF to a single person creates a version-control problem three months later, when a second party asks for the report and receives a different draft that nobody can prove was superseded.

sections.heading: What the Delay Actually Costs the Owner
paragraphs: The equipment stays down waiting on paper. A vessel held open pending a UT result, a tank out of service pending a floor scan report, a ship's survey held open pending thickness measurements. In every case the meter runs on the owner's side while the document runs on the contractor's side, and that split is the structural reason turnaround does not improve on its own no matter how many times it is raised in a kickoff meeting.

The costs are concrete and countable: extended isolation and blinding, scaffold rental, standby crews, deferred production, extended survey attendance, and in the worst case a repeat mobilisation because the access window closed. None of these appear on the inspection invoice, which is why they rarely enter the contractor selection decision at all and why the cheapest bid frequently produces the most expensive outage.

Owners who quantify one week of unavailability on a single unit find the number dwarfs the entire inspection scope's cost. That calculation, done once, changes how the scope of work is written and how bids are evaluated afterwards. It also reframes the [contractor selection checklist](/blog/choosing-an-ndt-service-provider-checklist) around systems capability and documentation throughput rather than day rate and crew size.

sections.heading: Writing Turnaround Into the Scope of Work
paragraphs: Set targets per stage, not one end-to-end figure. Name a deadline for the field advisory, a deadline for the reviewed draft, and a deadline for the issued signed report, each measured from the end of the shift in which the data was captured. A per-stage clock lets a late report be traced to the stage that slipped, which turns a dispute about blame into a conversation about a specific fixable handoff.

Split the deliverable deliberately. A field advisory carrying indication type, location, extent and the technician's preliminary call reaches the planning team the same shift and lets repair preparation start, while the formal report follows once the qualified reviewer has evaluated and signed. State in the scope that the advisory is preliminary and carries no acceptance decision, and the split creates speed without creating ambiguity about who decided what.

Ask bidders three operational questions: how data is captured in the field, how qualified review is queued and notified, and how many output templates are maintained by hand. The answers predict turnaround more reliably than any promised number in a bid document, because the promised number is a target while the workflow is a hard constraint on what the contractor can physically deliver.

sections.heading: Turnaround Is a Systems Problem With a Systems Fix
paragraphs: Every stage that shrinks does so for the same reason: a handoff between people or formats was removed. Structured capture removes transcription. Validation at entry removes the review-and-return loop. An electronic review queue removes the email wait. Multiple output templates from one record remove the re-keying. Electronic signature removes the geography. None of these change how an examination is performed or who is qualified to perform it.

The same data record that shortens the cycle also carries the fields that keep the report compliant, which is why faster reporting and lower rejection rates arrive together rather than trading against each other. The mandatory fields listed in ASME Section V become required fields in the form, and the [defects that get reports returned](/blog/ndt-report-format-what-clients-reject) become impossible to submit rather than something a coordinator catches on a good day.

Contractors carrying a turnaround problem across every client have a workflow problem, not a staffing problem, and hiring more coordinators makes the queue longer rather than shorter. Mapping the current cycle stage by stage, then removing handoffs, is what a [programme audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) produces. Owners who want the inspection record landing in a live asset model instead of a PDF folder should look at how [digital twin](/digital-twins) reporting closes the loop. faq.q: What is a reasonable turnaround for a routine NDT report?
faq.a: Set it per stage in the contract rather than accepting an end-to-end promise. A field advisory the same shift, a reviewed draft the next business day, and an issued signed report within a few business days of capture is achievable with structured field capture and an electronic review queue. A paper-and-transcription workflow cannot reach those numbers regardless of effort.

faq.q: Why does the contractor not just hire more report writers?
faq.a: Because transcription and qualified review are queue stages, and adding people to a queue lengthens the handoff chain rather than shortening the wait. The stages shrink when they are removed, not when they are staffed. Structured capture eliminates transcription outright. More coordinators redistribute the same work and add another handoff to the chain.

faq.q: Can I get results before the report is signed?
faq.a: Yes, as a preliminary field advisory carrying indication type, location, extent and the technician's call, clearly labelled as preliminary and carrying no acceptance decision. Repair planning starts on it. The acceptance decision waits for the qualified reviewer, as it must under any code that separates the examiner performing the work from the inspector evaluating the results.

faq.q: Does digital reporting create audit problems?
faq.a: It removes them. An electronic record captures the entry time, the entering technician's certification reference, the reviewer's identity and the approval timestamp automatically, which is a stronger evidentiary chain than a scanned signature on a typed page. Auditors accept it when the system controls access by role and preserves full revision history on every record.

faq.q: Where should the finished report live?
faq.a: In the owner's asset records, indexed to the component, rather than in an email thread. A report tied to a component identifier in an asset register or a digital model is retrievable at the next inspection interval by anyone who needs it. A PDF in a shared folder is retrievable only by the person who filed it, and only while they still work there.
